dedupe_keys.name: global flood impacts on ambulance and fire service accessibility now and under climate change loughborough thesis

description: This doctoral thesis assesses how river and coastal floods affect access to ambulance and fire services for people worldwide, now and under climate change. It was written by Sarah Johnson at Loughborough University and deposited in the university's repository in May 2024 under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives licence, free to download as a PDF. The framework restricts road networks with fluvial and coastal floods of 10-year and 100-year return periods, for 2010 and for 2050 under the RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 scenarios, and measures service area coverage and population reached within 8 and 30 minutes, with a Netherlands case on future service configurations. Coverage is global, with country results. Caveats: travel times are modelled, and the thesis is not peer reviewed as a whole. It estimates that 27 to 58 percent of the global population is within reach of ambulance services at baseline, falling to 20 to 48 percent under riverine flooding, and 14 to 35 percent for fire services; accessibility falls by 0.5 to 8 percent between 2010 and 2050; and hotspots lie in Asia and Africa, most often Bangladesh, Chad, Guyana and Liberia. Simulation uses: global baselines for flood exposure of emergency service coverage and climate adaptation planning. Related records: the England study (case_study-england-flood-disruption-emergency-response-vulnerable-populations) applies the method nationally.
